_about: Offline descriptions of common Windows / app / developer folders, compiled from publicly documented Windows and vendor behaviour. Patterns are matched against the lower-cased path with forward slashes ('?' = any single char, '*' = anything). First match wins, so specific patterns come first. Advice: Keep = do not delete; Safe to clear = contents regenerate; Review = check before deleting; Use tool = clean via the app/Windows setting.
rules: Virtual memory swap file used by Windows when RAM is full. Size is managed in System > Advanced > Performance > Virtual memory.
Holds RAM contents for hibernate / Fast Startup. Removed by running 'powercfg /h off' as admin.
Used by Store (UWP) apps for suspend/resume paging. Managed by Windows.
Boot-time crash dump stack log written by Windows.
Full crash dump written after a blue screen. Can be deleted via Disk Cleanup (System error memory dump files).

Side-by-side store of every Windows component version used for updates and repair. Much of its apparent size is hard links shared with System32, so real usage is smaller than shown. Shrink only with 'Dism /Online /Cleanup-Image /StartComponentCleanup' or Disk Cleanup.
Cached .msi/.msp packages needed to repair, update or uninstall installed programs. Deleting files breaks uninstall/repair.
Temporary storage for downloaded Windows updates. Cleared by Disk Cleanup (Windows Update Cleanup) or after updates install.
Windows Update working folder: downloads, history database and logs.
Trusted copies of all installed and staged device drivers. Old versions can be removed with pnputil or Disk Cleanup (Device driver packages).
Core 64-bit Windows system files, DLLs and tools.
32-bit system files used to run 32-bit programs on 64-bit Windows.
System-wide temporary files. Old contents can be cleared with Disk Cleanup / Storage Sense.
Small trace files Windows uses to speed up app launches. Rebuilt automatically.
Logs from setup, servicing (CBS), DISM, Windows Update, etc.
Built-in Windows UWP apps (Start, Settings shell parts, Edge components).
Windows servicing stack files used to install updates and features.
Diagnostic dumps from driver/kernel hangs (often GPU). Safe to delete old .dmp files.
Small crash dumps from blue screens; useful for diagnosing crashes, otherwise deletable.
Install location of Microsoft Store apps and games. Remove apps via Settings > Apps.
Installed 64-bit applications. Remove programs via Settings > Apps, not by deleting folders.
Installed 32-bit applications. Remove programs via Settings > Apps.
Installer bundles kept by Visual Studio / VC++ redistributables / WiX bundles for repair and uninstall.
Queued and archived crash reports. Safe to clear via Disk Cleanup.
Antivirus definitions, scan history and quarantine.
Docker Desktop images/volumes data. Clean with 'docker system prune'.
Anaconda Python distribution installed for all users.
Chocolatey package manager and installed packages.
Machine-wide application data and settings shared by all users (hidden).
Deleted files from this drive. Empty the Recycle Bin to free this space.
System Restore points, Volume Shadow Copies, indexing and dedup data. Manage via System Protection settings.
Old Windows installation kept after an upgrade (for rollback, ~10 days). Remove via Disk Cleanup > Previous Windows installation(s).
Temporary files from a Windows feature upgrade. Remove via Disk Cleanup (Temporary Windows installation files).
Temporary Windows setup/media files from an upgrade.
Temporary folder used while updating the recovery environment; normally empty after updates.
Leftovers from a 'Reset this PC' operation.
Local Microsoft Office installation source (older Office versions).
Extracted AMD driver installers; usually safe to delete after install.
Extracted NVIDIA driver installers; usually safe to delete after install.
Default install location for Xbox app / Game Pass PC games.
Your temporary files. Anything not in use can be deleted (Storage Sense / Disk Cleanup does this).
Cache for legacy IE/WebView/Office web content.
thumbcache_*.db files with Explorer thumbnails; rebuilt automatically.
Application crash dumps; safe to delete.
Compiled shader cache for games/apps; rebuilt automatically.
NVIDIA compiled shader cache; rebuilt automatically.
Contains ext4.vhdx - the virtual disk of your WSL Ubuntu Linux. Contents live inside the VHDX.
WhatsApp Desktop media, database and cache.
Per-app data folders for Microsoft Store (UWP) apps.
OneDrive client program and logs (not your synced files).
Microsoft Edge profiles: history, cache, extensions. Clear cache in Edge settings.
Google Chrome profiles: history, cache, extensions. Clear cache in Chrome settings.
Apps installed only for you (VS Code, Python, Discord, etc.). Uninstall via Settings > Apps.
Python pip download/wheel cache. Clear with 'pip cache purge'.
Node.js npm package cache. Clear with 'npm cache clean --force'.
Node.js npm package cache. Clear with 'npm cache clean --force'.
Yarn package cache. Clear with 'yarn cache clean'.
pnpm content-addressable package store. Clean with 'pnpm store prune'.
Docker Desktop WSL disk images. Clean with 'docker system prune'.
Android SDK, emulator images and build tools.
IDE caches and indexes for IntelliJ/PyCharm etc.; rebuilt on demand.
Microsoft Teams classic cache; clearing it resets the local cache.
Visual Studio Code settings, caches and workspace storage.
Zoom client data; local recordings may be elsewhere (Documents/Zoom).
Telegram Desktop data and cache. Clear cache in Telegram settings.
Machine-specific application data and caches for this user (hidden). Large subfolders are often caches.
App data for low-integrity (sandboxed) apps, e.g. Java, some games, browsers.
Application settings for this user that can roam with the profile.
Hidden per-user application data (settings, caches, app-installed programs).
Your OneDrive synced folder. Cloud-only files take no local space (shown separately). Deleting here deletes from the cloud too.
Google Drive synced folder. Deleting here deletes from the cloud too.
Dropbox synced folder. Deleting here deletes from the cloud too.
Files downloaded by browsers and apps; often holds old installers and duplicates.
Your pictures library (also Screenshots, Camera Roll).
Your videos library (also Captures from Game Bar).
Cross-tool cache folder (Hugging Face models, pip, pre-commit, etc.).
Conda environments and package cache for this user.
Anaconda Python distribution; 'conda clean --all' frees cached packages.
Miniconda Python distribution; 'conda clean --all' frees cached packages.
.NET NuGet global package cache. Clear with 'dotnet nuget locals all --clear'.
Gradle build caches and wrapper distributions.
Android emulator AVD images and adb keys.
Downloaded local LLM model files for Ollama.
Rust Cargo registry cache and installed binaries.
Your user registry (NTUSER.DAT) and its logs.
Files shared between all users of this PC.
Template copied to create new user profiles.
All user profiles on this PC.
Node.js project dependencies; recreated with 'npm install'. Safe to delete for inactive projects.
Version history of a Git repository. Deleting it loses history.
Project Python virtual environment; recreatable from requirements.
Project Python virtual environment; recreatable from requirements.
Next.js build output and cache; regenerated by build.
Compiled debug build output; regenerated by building.
.NET/C++ intermediate build files; regenerated by building.
Rust/Maven build output folder (if inside a project).
Visual Studio solution user options and IntelliSense DB; regenerated.
Installed Steam games. Uninstall from the Steam library.
Pre-compiled shaders for Steam games; rebuilt as needed.
Steam library folder (games, workshop content, caches).
Photos and videos from camera apps or phone import.
Xbox Game Bar screenshots and video recordings.
Standard camera folder (copied from a phone or camera).
Duplicate copies moved here by Storage Explorer's 'Identical files' page (one sub-folder per run, original paths kept). Undo a run from the app, or delete the run folder once you are sure.
Windows File History backup versions. Manage via Control Panel > File History.
System image created by 'Backup and Restore (Windows 7)'.
Folder named as a backup - check the Backup roots tab to see what it duplicates.
Folder named as a backup - check the Backup roots tab to see what it duplicates.
Folder named 'old' - often an outdated copy.
Folder created by Explorer copy-paste ('- Copy'); likely a duplicate.
